name: Lion Monument
overview: The Lion Monument (Löwendenkmal) is a rock relief carved in sandstone commemorating the Swiss Guards who were massacred during the French Revolution. Mark Twain called it 'the most mournful and moving piece of stone in the world.'
history: This heart-wrenching sculpture commemorates one of history's most heroic last stands. On August 10, 1792, during the French Revolution, 786 Swiss Guards defended King Louis XVI at the Tuileries Palace in Paris as revolutionary mobs stormed the gates. Despite the King ordering them to cease fire, these loyal soldiers fought to their deaths rather than abandon their posts - Swiss honor demanded it. Only about 100 survived the massacre. The monument shows a dying lion, pierced by a spear, lying over the French royal coat of arms, symbolizing their faithful sacrifice. Designed by famous Danish sculptor Bertel Thorvaldsen and carved directly into a sandstone cliff by Lukas Ahorn, it took two years to complete. Mark Twain called it 'the most mournful and moving piece of stone in the world,' and many visitors are moved to tears. This tragedy led to Switzerland's permanent neutrality - never again would Swiss blood be spilled for foreign powers. The monument reflects the Swiss values of loyalty, honor, and sacrifice that still define the nation today.
highlights: Dying lion carved into natural rock face
Shield with fleur-de-lis representing French royalty
Names of officers and casualty numbers inscribed
tips: Free to visit and accessible year-round. Best photographed in soft morning or evening light. Small parking area available. Combine with nearby Glacier Garden visit. Very emotional and moving monument.
